The LBNL report estimates U.S. data centers used 192 TWh in 2024, or 4.7% of U.S. electricity.
Qualification: A modeled historical estimate for all data centers within the report’s scope, not AI workloads alone. Cryptocurrency mining is excluded.
Primary sources: https://www.energy.gov/documents/united-states-data-center-energy-usage-report-2025-update
evidence.evidence/8f5981b37d3405a8ca1e45cf1eaf3b1:
The LBNL 2030 reference projection is 649 TWh; a compounded sensitivity stress-test range spans 521–843 TWh.
Qualification: Projection assumptions use late-2025 information. The stress-test range is not a probabilistic confidence interval and does not capture every structural discontinuity; it is neither observed demand nor committed project load.
Primary sources: https://www.energy.gov/documents/united-states-data-center-energy-usage-report-2025-update
evidence.evidence/106cb6094e9a0174e50166be56942f7:
The IEA’s 2026 executive summary projects global data-center electricity use rising from 485 TWh in 2025 to about 950 TWh in 2030.
Qualification: A global projection; it cannot be substituted for a U.S. forecast or a local grid impact study. It concerns all data centers, not exclusively AI workloads. IEA and LBNL models are not one harmonized dataset.
Primary sources: https://www.iea.org/reports/key-questions-on-energy-and-ai/executive-summary
evidence.evidence/156060d20ccdd842507363179ca90e0:
Annual TWh cannot by itself determine a proposed facility’s peak MW demand, interconnection cost or reliability impact. Local load shape and engineering evidence are necessary.
Qualification: Analytical distinction; no site-specific engineering determination is made.
Primary sources: https://www.energy.gov/documents/united-states-data-center-energy-usage-report-2025-update | https://www.iea.org/reports/key-questions-on-energy-and-ai/executive-summary
